procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order, dated July 20, 1967 of the Allahabad High Court in Cr. A. No. 469 of 1967 and Ref. No. 21 of 1967.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant appealed in the High Court of Allahabad and the Tempy. Sessions Judge also made a reference for confirmation of the sentence of death. The High Court dismissed the appeal, accepted the reference and confirmed the sentence of death.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant has now come up to this Court against that judgment of the High Court in appeal by special leave. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and ordered a retrial.

directions: The appellant shall be tried afresh for this charge after complying with the requirements of law.
The case is remanded to the Court of Session for this purpose.

issue.issue_text: Whether Rule 37 of the General Rules (Criminal), 1957, promulgated by the Allahabad High Court, is a statutory rule with binding force.

facts: Rule 37 of the General Rules (Criminal), 1957, was promulgated by the High Court of Allahabad.
The High Court created these rules in the exercise of powers granted to it by Article 227 of the Constitution and Section 554 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The rules were officially published in the Government Gazette with the previous approval of the Government of Uttar Pradesh, as stated in the notification.
law: Rules created by a subordinate legislative authority (like a High Court) in the exercise of delegated powers granted by the Constitution or a statute are considered "law".
Such rules can supplement the procedure laid down in the Code of Criminal Procedure without being in conflict with it.
application: The Court examined the notification under which the rules were published and found it clearly stated that the High Court was acting under the powers conferred on it by the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Code.
Because the rules were framed using these constitutional and statutory powers, the Court reasoned that they are "clearly statutory Rules."
The Court rejected the argument that the rule was not "law" because it wasn't made by a legislature, citing precedents that rules made by a delegated authority are indeed considered law.
The Court also determined that Rule 37 supplements the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code (specifically Section 340) and is not in conflict with it, thus upholding its validity.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that Rule 37 is a statutory rule with binding force and, as such, it forms a part of the mandatory procedure for the trial of criminal cases in courts subordinate to the Allahabad High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the direction in Rule 37 to appoint counsel for an accused in a capital case is mandatory, despite the use of the word 'may'.

law.name: Rule 37 of the General Rules (Criminal) 1957
law.description: A statutory rule, made by the High Court, which states that a court 'may' engage counsel at state expense for an accused person in a capital case if they have not engaged counsel themselves and do not have sufficient means to do so.

law.name: Section 340, Criminal Procedure Code (Cr. P.C.)
law.description: A provision that gives an accused the right to be defended by a lawyer, but does not by itself create a mandatory duty for the court to provide one at state expense.

application.description: The Court first determined the nature and purpose of Rule 37. It held that the rule is statutory and forms a part of the established procedure for criminal trials.

The Court focused on the intention behind the rule, which is to ensure that no accused person faces a trial for a capital offense without legal representation. It reasoned that interpreting the word 'may' as merely optional or discretionary would "completely defeat" this fundamental purpose.

The Court explained that the word 'may' was used not to give the court discretion, but because the appointment of counsel is dependent on certain pre-conditions being met: namely, that the accused has not engaged their own counsel and lacks the means to do so. Once these conditions are satisfied, the Court's duty to appoint counsel becomes mandatory.

The Court addressed the State's argument that Rule 37 conflicted with Section 340 of the Cr. P.C. It clarified that the rule does not conflict with the section but rather supplements it. While Section 340 does not mandate the appointment of counsel, it also does not prohibit it. Rule 37 simply adds a mandatory requirement in the specific context of capital cases.

The Court also rejected the argument that the accused must prove they were prejudiced by the failure to appoint counsel. It held that when a person's life is at stake, the failure to comply with the prescribed legal procedure is a fundamental flaw in itself, and the question of prejudice does not arise.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that despite the use of the word 'may', Rule 37 imposes a mandatory duty on the court to appoint counsel for an unrepresented accused in a capital case, provided the conditions laid down in the rule are met. The Court's decision was based on the rule's clear purpose to prevent any accused from facing a capital charge without legal representation.

issue.issue_text: Whether the failure to provide sufficient time to the appointed counsel to prepare for the defence, as required by Rule 37, vitiates the trial.

facts: An advocate was appointed by the Sessions Court to defend the appellant, who was facing a murder charge, on the very same day the trial was scheduled to begin.
The trial commenced immediately after the counsel's appointment, and witnesses were examined.
The record did not show that the counsel asked for more time, but the court deemed this immaterial.
Later, the counsel applied to recall the sole eyewitness for further cross-examination, stating the initial cross-examination was ineffective, but this application was rejected.
law: Rule 37 of the General Rules (Criminal) 1957 is a mandatory statutory rule that forms part of the procedure for criminal trials.
This rule requires that counsel appointed for an accused facing a capital charge must be allowed "sufficient time to prepare for the defence."
The rule places a positive duty on the court to grant this time, regardless of whether the counsel makes a specific request.

The procedure established by law under Article 21 of the Constitution includes such statutory rules, and depriving a citizen of life without complying with this procedure is a violation of Article 21.
application: The Court determined that appointing counsel just before the trial started constituted a clear failure to comply with the requirement of Rule 37.
It held that a "mere formal compliance" with the rule is not enough; the purpose is to give the accused a real opportunity to defend, which requires adequate preparation time.

The Court rejected the argument that the appellant needed to show prejudice. It reasoned that when a citizen is deprived of life without following the prescribed legal procedure, the question of prejudice does not arise.
Alternatively, the Court stated that when sufficient time for preparation is not granted, prejudice "must necessarily be inferred."
The Court also found that actual prejudice was evident from the counsel's later attempt to recall a key witness, which showed he felt unprepared during the initial examination.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the failure to provide the appointed counsel with sufficient time to prepare the defense was a violation of the mandatory procedure established by Rule 37. This non-compliance deprived the accused of a fair opportunity to defend himself, thereby vitiating the entire trial.

issue.issue_text: Whether a conviction can be upheld if no prejudice is shown to have been caused to the accused by the failure to comply with the mandatory procedure prescribed by law.

facts: An amicus curiae counsel was appointed to represent the appellant on the same day the trial was set to begin.
This belated appointment did not provide the counsel sufficient time to prepare the defense, which violated a mandatory procedural rule.
The opposing counsel argued that the conviction should be upheld because it was not shown that this procedural failure caused any specific prejudice to the appellant.
law: Article 21 of the Constitution states that no person shall be deprived of their life or personal liberty except according to the "procedure established by law."
This "procedure established by law" includes mandatory procedural rules, such as those requiring that counsel be given sufficient time to prepare a defense.
application: The Court held that when a citizen is deprived of life without complying with the mandatory procedure prescribed by law, the question of prejudice does not arise.
The failure to follow the prescribed procedure is, in itself, a violation of the fundamental right under Article 21.
The Court stated that practices that do not allow counsel adequate time for preparation reduce the right to counsel to a "farce."
As a secondary point, the Court also found that prejudice did, in fact, exist and could be "necessarily inferred" from the failure to grant counsel sufficient time to prepare the defense.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that a conviction is void if a mandatory procedure prescribed by law is not followed in a case involving the deprivation of life. In such a fundamental breach of procedure, which violates Article 21, the question of whether the accused suffered prejudice is irrelevant.

issue.issue_text: Whether a breach of procedure laid down by subordinate legislation (like Rule 37) amounts to a breach of Article 21 of the Constitution.

facts: The appellant was sentenced to death in a trial where the defense counsel was appointed just as the trial was about to begin.
This belated appointment violated Rule 37 of the General Rules (Criminals), 1957, which requires that counsel be given sufficient time to prepare the defense.
Rule 37 was a form of subordinate legislation, promulgated by the High Court under its powers from Article 227 of the Constitution and the Code of Criminal Procedure.
law: Article 21 of the Constitution states that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to 'procedure established by law'.
The central legal question was whether the word 'law' in Article 21 includes only acts of the legislature or also covers subordinate legislation, like rules made by a delegated authority.
The Court rejected an earlier, narrow interpretation from *A. K. Gopalan's case* which suggested 'law' meant only enacted law.

Citing later precedents like *Maqbool Hussain*, *Pandit M. S. M. Sharma*, and *Makhan Singh*, the Court affirmed that the word 'law' in Article 21 does include rules made by a subordinate legislative authority in exercise of its delegated powers.
application: The Court identified Rule 37 as a valid rule created by the High Court in the exercise of its delegated legislative power under the Constitution and the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Because subordinate legislation is considered 'law' for the purposes of Article 21, Rule 37 forms part of the 'procedure established by law'.
The trial was conducted in violation of Rule 37, as the counsel was not given sufficient time to prepare.
Therefore, the procedure followed by the trial court was not in accordance with the 'procedure established by law'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a breach of procedure laid down by subordinate legislation, such as Rule 37, is a breach of the 'procedure established by law' under Article 21. Consequently, the conviction and death sentence, having been awarded in a trial that violated this procedure, resulted in a deprivation of the appellant's life in breach of his fundamental right under Article 21.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Rule 37 of the General Rules (Criminal), 1957, promulgated by the Allahabad High Court, is a statutory rule with binding force.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's entire claim is based on the rights conferred by Rule 37, implying it is a binding statutory rule that forms part of the procedure for trial.
respondent_arguments: Rule 37 was not enacted by a legislature and therefore should not be considered part of the 'procedure established by law'.
Rule 37 is void because it contravenes the principle laid down in Section 340 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the direction in Rule 37 to appoint counsel for an accused in a capital case is mandatory, despite the use of the word 'may'.
appellant_arguments: The non-compliance with the rule, which is the basis of the appeal, implies that the appellant considers its provisions to be mandatory.
respondent_arguments: Based on the use of the word 'may', the rule should be interpreted as enabling or discretionary, not mandatory.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the failure to provide sufficient time to the appointed counsel to prepare for the defence, as required by Rule 37, vitiates the trial.
appellant_arguments: The trial was vitiated because the last clause of Rule 37 was breached, as the appointed counsel was not allowed sufficient time to prepare the defence.
The counsel's application to recall a key witness shows he felt unprepared to cross-examine properly due to the lack of time.
respondent_arguments: The text does not contain a specific counter-argument from the respondent on this point, beyond the general argument that the conviction should be upheld.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a conviction can be upheld if no prejudice is shown to have been caused to the accused by the failure to comply with the mandatory procedure prescribed by law.
appellant_arguments: Prejudice was, in fact, caused, as demonstrated by the counsel's inability to properly cross-examine the sole eye-witness.
The question of prejudice does not arise when a citizen is deprived of life without complying with the mandatory procedure prescribed by law.
respondent_arguments: The conviction and sentence should not be held void because it has not been shown that any prejudice was caused to the appellant by the failure to observe the procedure.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a breach of procedure laid down by subordinate legislation (like Rule 37) amounts to a breach of Article 21 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The breach of Rule 37, a statutory rule, constitutes a violation of the 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The sentence should not be considered a breach of Article 21 because Rule 37 was not enacted by any legislature and, therefore, is not part of the 'procedure established by law'.

cases.case_name: Maqbool Hussain v. The State of Bombay & Connected Cases
cases.principle: The word 'law' in Article 21 includes subordinate legislation, such as rules framed by the government under a statute.

cases.case_name: Pandit M. S. M. Sharma v. Shri Sri Krishna Sinha and Others
cases.principle: Rules made by a Legislature under the Constitution are 'law' justifying the deprivation of personal liberty guaranteed by Article 21.

cases.case_name: Makhan Singh v. State of Punjab & Connected Appeals
cases.principle: Rules made by the Central Government under an ordinance are 'law' for the purposes of Article 21.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Rules made by a subordinate legislative authority, such as a High Court, under its delegated constitutional or statutory powers constitute 'law' for the purposes of Article 21. A trial held in violation of a mandatory procedural rule, which provides for legal representation in cases involving a capital sentence, results in the deprivation of life contrary to the procedure established by law. Such a rule is to be interpreted as mandatory, even if it uses the word 'may', if a discretionary interpretation would defeat its fundamental purpose. When such a mandatory procedure is violated, the conviction is void, and the question of whether the accused suffered prejudice does not arise.
obiter: In this specific case, the facts indicate that there was, in fact, prejudice to the accused caused by the non-compliance with the requirement of the rule.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that Rule 37 of the General Rules (Criminal), 1957, is a mandatory statutory rule that forms part of the 'procedure established by law' under Article 21. The failure of the trial court to provide counsel, appointed for an accused in a capital case, with sufficient time to prepare the defence constitutes a fundamental procedural breach. This violation is so severe that it vitiates the entire trial, rendering the conviction and sentence void regardless of whether specific prejudice is proven, as it denies the accused a fair and reasonable opportunity to prove their innocence and amounts to a deprivation of life without due process.
legal_tests_applied: Purposive Interpretation of Statutes: The court interpreted the word 'may' as mandatory ('must') by looking at the rule's underlying purpose, concluding that a discretionary reading would 'be completely defeated' as the rule's intent is to ensure no accused in a capital case is unrepresented.

Per Se Prejudice Rule for Fundamental Procedural Breaches: The court explicitly rejected the need to prove actual prejudice from the procedural violation, stating, 'the question of prejudice does not arise when a citizen is deprived of his life without complying with the procedure prescribed by law.'

Substantive vs. Formal Compliance: The court held that procedural rules for fair trials require more than token adherence, stating that 'a mere formal compliance with this Rule will not carry out the object underlying the rule' and that providing insufficient time for preparation reduces the process to a 'farce'.
why_appellant_lost: The State's argument that Rule 37 is merely discretionary because it uses the word 'may' was rejected; the court held that the purpose of the rule makes it a 'mandatory direction' once its pre-conditions are met.

The State's argument that the conviction should be upheld because no prejudice was shown was rejected on the principle that failure to comply with mandatory procedure in a capital case is an intrinsic violation of justice that does not require a separate showing of prejudice.

The State's argument that Rule 37 is not part of the 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 because it was not enacted by a legislature was rejected, as the court found it to be a binding 'statutory rule' whose violation led to the quashing of the conviction.

The State's argument that Rule 37 was void for contravening Section 340 of the Criminal Procedure Code was rejected, with the court holding that the rule 'only supplements the provision' and is 'in no way in conflict' with it.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that Rule 37 is a binding 'statutory rule' because it was promulgated by the High Court in the exercise of its powers under Article 227 of the Constitution and Section 554 of the Criminal Procedure Code, making it part of the 'procedure for trial'.

The court accepted that the failure to provide the appointed counsel sufficient time to prepare for the defence was a fatal flaw, finding that 'the time given was insufficient and, in the circumstances, no real opportunity was given to the accused to defend himself.'

The court accepted that the breach of a mandatory statutory rule like Rule 37, which is part of the procedure for trial, constitutes a violation of the 'procedure prescribed by law,' thereby implicating Article 21 when a person's life is at stake.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning is grounded in the policy that 'no accused person should remain totally unrepresented by a lawyer, if he is being tried on a charge for which a capital sentence can be awarded.'

The court emphasized that the right to counsel must be effective, not illusory, stating that inadequate preparation time would 'reduce to a farce the engagement of counsel... which has been made for the purpose of effectively carrying out the duty cast on courts of law to see that no one is deprived of life and liberty without a fair and reasonable opportunity being afforded to him to prove his innocence.'
